title: Promises & Async/Await
tagline: From the thenable contract to production concurrency: chaining, errors, async/await, and the patterns that survive on-call.

lessons.title: Promise States and the Thenable Contract
lessons.comparisonNote: Java's `CompletableFuture` is the direct parallel: `supplyAsync` ~ the promise executor, `thenApply` ~ `then`, `exceptionally` ~ `catch`. Two differences that matter. First, a JS promise's executor starts *immediately* at construction; a `CompletableFuture` pipeline stage only runs when you build it (and `supplyAsync` needs an explicit executor — JS has no executor choice; there's one microtask queue). Second, JS promises are not cancellable — there is no `cancel()`; cancellation is a separate cooperative protocol (`AbortController`, last lesson). `CompletableFuture.cancel` exists but is advisory and rarely effective — both ecosystems end up hand-rolling cancellation.
keyPoints: States: pending → fulfilled | rejected; settlement is final — later resolve/reject calls are ignored.
The executor runs synchronously at construction; only `.then` callbacks are deferred (microtasks).
Any object with `.then` is a thenable and gets assimilated — the interop contract behind `await` and `Promise.resolve`.
Never pass an `async` executor: its rejections are silently dropped (unhandled rejection).

lessons.title: Chaining, Error Propagation, Unhandled Rejections
lessons.body:
# Chaining, Error Propagation, Unhandled Rejections

## `.then` always returns a new promise

This single fact *is* the chaining model:

- return a **value** → the new promise fulfills with it
- return a **promise/thenable** → the new promise adopts its state (flattening — no nested promises)
- **throw** → the new promise rejects with the thrown error

```js
fetchUser(1)
  .then(user => fetchOrders(user.id)) // returns a promise → adopted
  .then(orders => orders.length)      // returns a value → fulfilled with it
  .then(n => console.log(`orders: ${n}`));
```

Each `.then` is a link; values flow forward, and the chain never nests.

## Errors propagate like exceptions — with one trap

A rejection skips forward past fulfillment handlers to the next rejection handler, exactly like an exception unwinding to the nearest `catch`. But these two are *not* the same:

```js
p.then(onFulfilled).catch(onRejected); // catch handles rejections from p AND throws inside onFulfilled
p.then(onFulfilled, onRejected);       // onRejected handles p only — a throw inside onFulfilled escapes!
```

The two-argument form is the trap: it looks equivalent and isn't. Prefer `.then(...).catch(...)` unless you deliberately want the narrower scope.

## Unhandled rejections: the production footgun

If a promise rejects and no rejection handler is attached by the end of the microtask checkpoint, the runtime fires `unhandledrejection`. In browsers that's a console error; **in Node it's fatal by default** — an unhandled rejection crashes the process. Common ways to trigger it:

- Fire-and-forget: `doAsyncWork();` with no `.catch` — if it ever rejects, the process dies.
- Attaching `.catch` too late: `const p = work(); await somethingElse(); p.catch(...)` — if `p` rejected during the await, the unhandled rejection already fired.
- The async-executor pitfall from the previous lesson.

Defense: every promise chain ends in `.catch` (or is awaited inside `try/catch`), and lint rules (`no-floating-promises`) catch the fire-and-forget case in TypeScript codebases.

## `finally`

`.finally(cb)` runs on settlement either way and passes the original value/reason through — for cleanup, not transformation. Returning a promise from `finally` *does* delay the chain, but the settlement value is preserved.
lessons.comparisonNote: This maps directly onto Java's exception discipline: `.then` / `.catch` / `.finally` are `try` / `catch` / `finally` stretched across time. The critical difference is *where* the 'stack' lives — in Java the call stack carries the exception to the handler; in JS the chain does, which is why attaching a handler *late* (after an await boundary) misses: the rejection already propagated past with nobody listening. And the stakes differ: an uncaught exception kills one Java thread, but an unhandled rejection kills the whole Node process by default.
keyPoints: `.then` returns a new promise: values fulfill it, returned promises are adopted, throws reject it.
Rejections skip to the next rejection handler; `.then(a).catch(b)` is wider than `.then(a, b)` — the two-arg form won't catch `a`'s own throw.
In Node, an unhandled rejection crashes the process — end every chain in `.catch` or `try/catch`.
`.finally` is for cleanup: it can't transform the value, but a returned promise delays the chain.

lessons.title: async/await: Desugaring, Sequential vs Parallel
lessons.comparisonNote: Think of `await` as `Future.get()` that doesn't block the thread: `get()` parks the *thread* until the value arrives; `await` parks only the async function's *continuation* and frees the event loop for everything else. (Java 21's virtual threads attack the same problem from the other side — making blocking cheap.) And the sequential-await bug has a direct Java analog: calling `future.get()` inside a loop instead of collecting futures and joining them. `CompletableFuture.thenCompose` ~ `await` chaining; `thenCombine` / `allOf` ~ awaiting multiple promises.
keyPoints: `await` parks the function's continuation as a microtask; an `async` function always returns a promise.
`await` in a loop serializes independent work — start all promises first, combine with `Promise.all`.
`try/catch` around `await` handles rejection; for partial-failure batches use `allSettled` or per-item `.catch`.
Even `await 42` yields asynchronously — `await` is never synchronous.

lessons.title: Concurrency Control: all/race/allSettled/any, Limiters, Retry, Cancellation
lessons.comparisonNote: Java's `ExecutorService` with a fixed thread pool *is* the concurrency limiter — bounded parallelism is the default mental model in Java, while in JS you have to build it (hence p-limit). `CompletableFuture.allOf` ~ `Promise.all`, except `allOf` yields `Void` and you re-join values manually — `Promise.all` handing you the ordered values array is genuinely nicer. `orTimeout` ~ `AbortSignal.timeout`. Retry has no stdlib answer in either language — everyone hand-rolls it, which is exactly why interviewers ask you to.
keyPoints: `all` fails fast with ordered values; `allSettled` never rejects; `race` takes the first settlement; `any` takes the first fulfillment (`AggregateError` if all fail).
Bounded concurrency (p-limit style) protects sockets, memory, and rate limits — `Promise.all` on unbounded input is a production incident.
Retry transient failures with exponential backoff + jitter, only for idempotent operations.
Cancellation is cooperative via `AbortController`; `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` replaces the race-with-timer pattern.

exercises.title: Promise.all from scratch
hints: Wrap each entry with `Promise.resolve(entry)` — that one call handles plain values, native promises, and thenables.
Store each fulfillment at its *index* and count down `remaining`; resolve only when it hits zero — that's what preserves input order.
Reject on the first failure and guard the handlers with a `settled` flag so late fulfillments after a rejection are ignored.

exercises.title: Concurrency limiter (p-limit)
hints: Keep two pieces of state: `active` (running count) and `queue` (waiting `{fn, resolve, reject}` entries).
Every completion path must do three things: `active--`, settle the queued promise, and call `next()` to pull the next waiter.
Don't forget the rejection path — an unhandled task rejection inside the limiter would hang that slot's promise forever.

exercises.title: Retry with backoff
hints: `await fn()` handles both sync throws and async rejections uniformly — no need to branch.
The delay for attempt index `i` is `baseDelayMs * 2 ** i`: 50, 100, 200... Don't sleep after the final attempt — just throw.
Remember the last error in a variable; after the loop, `throw lastError` preserves the original failure for the caller.

exercises.title: AbortController cancellation demo
hints: Always `clearTimeout` in the abort listener — otherwise the timer keeps the event loop (and the closure) alive.
`signal.reason` carries *why* it aborted: your custom `DOMException` for manual aborts, a `TimeoutError` for `AbortSignal.timeout`.
Check `signal.aborted` up front: a task started with an already-aborted signal must reject immediately, not start the timer.
